title: Practice Project: Student Profile
summary: Put everything together! Build your first complete multi-object Java program step by step with a guided project and verify your Module 1 mastery.
learningObjectives: Design and write a complete Student class with 4 properties and a formatted displayProfile() method
Instantiate multiple student objects, populate their data, and run their behaviors
Complete the 10-point Module 1 Mastery Checkpoint with total confidence
expectedOutcomes: A working, portfolio-ready Student Profile program written independently
The satisfying realization: 'I can actually write classes and create objects in Java!'

activities.title: Welcome to Your First OOP Build!

analogy.headline: You have transitioned from writing scripts to architecting programs
analogy.story:
Think back to when you first started Java. Everything was packed into one giant `main` method with loose variables and print statements.

Now, you are thinking like a real software engineer. You design an entity (`Student`), declare what it knows (state), define what it does (behavior), and create multiple living instances of it.

This guided project will walk you through building your very own Student Profile system from a blank canvas. Let's build it together step by step!
analogy.keyTakeaway: You are not copying code. You are engineering a clean, reusable system using classes and objects.

activities.title: Step-by-Step Project Roadmap

keyTakeaways: Follow the 7-step architecture: Blueprint -> Fields -> Behaviors -> Instantiation -> Population -> Execution -> Extension
Encapsulate display logic inside displayProfile() for clean caller code
Instantiate multiple distinct student objects to observe state independence
Extend with custom attributes (like city or grade) to customize your build

activities.content:
Here is the exact 7-step roadmap to build your Student Profile project:

```text
Step 1: Declare the class blueprint
   class Student { ... }

Step 2: Add the 4 properties
   String name;
   int age;
   String course;
   double marks;

Step 3: Add the displayProfile() method
   Prints a clean, formatted student profile card

Step 4: Create the first Student object
   Student student1 = new Student();
   Set Rahul's details (Age 20, Course Java, Marks 85.5)

Step 5: Create the second Student object
   Student student2 = new Student();
   Set Priya's details (Age 21, Course Python, Marks 91.0)

Step 6: Run and inspect the output!
   Verify that each student card displays its own unique data

Step 7: Personal Extension Challenge
   Add a custom field (like String city or char grade) and create a 3rd student!
```

### Expected Output:
```text
--- Student Profile ---
Name: Rahul
Age: 20
Course: Java
Marks: 85.5

--- Student Profile ---
Name: Priya
Age: 21
Course: Python
Marks: 91.0
```

Take it step by step. You already know every single concept needed to build this!

activities.title: Full Solution Walkthrough
activities.description: Notice how clean and readable this code is! Any programmer looking at this immediately understands what a Student is and how student records are created and displayed.

questions.prompt: If you want to add an 'email' property to all students in your program, where should you declare 'String email;'?
options: Inside the main method as a loose variable
Inside the Student class blueprint, so all current and future student objects automatically get the field
In the operating system terminal
Inside a System.out.println statement
questions.explanation: Adding the field to the Student class immediately upgrades the blueprint for all student objects.

questions.prompt: What is the core takeaway of Module 1: Classes & Objects?
options: Classes are blueprints defining properties and behaviors; objects are living instances created with 'new' holding independent state
OOP means writing 500 lines inside a single main method
Java code should never declare variables
Methods can only be called on Tuesdays
questions.explanation: Classes are the template; objects are the real, living instances bundling state and behavior together.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of steps when building an OOP program?
options: 1. Define the class blueprint -> 2. Instantiate objects with 'new' -> 3. Populate state and invoke behaviors
1. Call methods -> 2. Turn off the computer -> 3. Write the class
1. Create objects -> 2. Hope the class creates itself
1. Write the main method only without classes
questions.explanation: First design the class blueprint, then instantiate objects in main, then interact with them.

questions.prompt: Why is 'student1.displayProfile()' cleaner than passing 4 arguments to a static print method?
options: Because student1 already encapsulates its own name, age, course, and marks
Because it uses zero lines of code
Because Java doesn't allow printing numbers
Because static methods are illegal in Java
questions.explanation: The student object already has access to all its internal fields, making method calls clean and argument-free.

questions.prompt: In our Student Profile project, what will happen if we don't assign 'student1.marks = 85.5;'?
options: The program will crash with an explosion
The marks field will default to 0.0 without crashing
Java will guess Rahul's marks using AI
The computer will shut down
questions.explanation: Primitive double fields in a Java object default safely to 0.0 if not explicitly assigned.

questions.prompt: What is the output when student1 (name: Rahul) and student2 (name: Priya) both call displayProfile()?
options: Both print Rahul
Both print Priya
student1 prints Rahul's card, and student2 prints Priya's card
Nothing is printed
questions.explanation: Each object's displayProfile() method prints that specific object's private field values.

hints.hint: Each object uses its own state.

questions.prompt: When creating a third student (student3), do we need to write a new class?
options: Yes, you must write class Student3
No! We simply instantiate another object using: Student student3 = new Student();
Yes, every object needs its own class file
Only if student3 is studying Python
questions.explanation: A single class blueprint can create as many objects as you want. You never write duplicate classes for new instances!

questions.prompt: Can a method inside Student format its output with custom headers and spacing?
options: Yes, methods can use System.out.println() with any desired formatting, lines, and borders
No, methods can only return numbers
Only if you install external UI libraries
Only in web browsers
questions.explanation: Methods have full access to standard Java printing and formatting capabilities.

questions.prompt: If you want to calculate if a student passed (marks >= 40.0), where should that method live?
options: Inside the Student class as: boolean isPassed() { return marks >= 40.0; }
Outside in a random text file
In your web browser bookmarks
Inside an operating system setting
questions.explanation: Because marks belongs to the Student, the calculation logic should live inside the Student class as a behavior.

hints.hint: Keep logic where the data lives.

questions.prompt: How should you feel after completing Module 1?
options: Confused and overwhelmed by 50 textbook terms
Empowered and confident: I understand what classes and objects are, why OOP exists, and I can build simple OOP programs independently!
Afraid to write Java code
Convinced that OOP is only for university professors
questions.explanation: You now genuinely understand the core mental model of OOP and can write real classes and objects!

interviewQA.question: Walk me through how you would model a Student in an object-oriented system.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: I start by creating a Student class as a blueprint. Inside, I declare its state using instance variables like name, age, course, and marks. Then I add behaviors as methods, such as displayProfile() or calculateGrade(). In my application, whenever a new student registers, I use 'new Student()' to instantiate a fresh object and populate their unique details.
keyPoints: Define class as blueprint with state (fields)
Instantiate objects with 'new' and set unique data

interviewQA.question: Why is it better to put displayProfile() inside the Student class rather than in Main?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It adheres to object autonomy: the Student entity knows its own data and should know how to present itself. This eliminates the need to pass 4 different parameters from Main into a separate formatting method.
keyPoints: Clean and readable code in Main

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between a class definition and object execution?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Class definition occurs at compile time when you write the template in code. Object execution occurs at runtime when the JVM encounters 'new ClassName()', allocates memory, and executes method instructions.
keyPoints: Compile time definition vs runtime memory allocation
Classes are static code; objects are dynamic running entities

interviewQA.question: Can a class have another object as a field in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes! While we only used simple types like String and int in Module 1, a class can easily hold other object references (such as Student having an Address object). That is called object composition, which is covered in upcoming modules.
keyPoints: Object composition allows rich domain modeling
Classes can contain references to other objects

interviewQA.question: What are the common beginner mistakes when writing classes and objects?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer:
1. Forgetting to use 'new' and getting NullPointerException.
2. Writing methods outside the class.
3. Confusing the class name with the object reference variable name.
4. Re-declaring class fields inside methods accidentally.
keyPoints: Confusing class name vs variable name

interviewQA.question: How would you explain the value of OOP to a team that only writes procedural scripts?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: OOP pays huge dividends as soon as your project grows. It prevents bugs from scattered variables, makes code intuitive to understand because it reflects real-world entities, and allows different developers to work on different classes simultaneously without stepping on each other's toes.
keyPoints: Enables clean team division of labor

interviewQA.question: What did you learn in Module 1 that prepares you for Module 2 (Constructors)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In Module 1, we learned that after creating an object with 'new Student()', we had to manually set every field line-by-line: s.name = 'Rahul'; s.age = 20; etc. This reveals why Constructors exist: Constructors let us pass these values at the exact moment of creation in a single line!
keyPoints: Understood the pain of manual property assignment
Sets up natural motivation for Constructors in Module 2

activities.title: Module 1 Mastery Checkpoint (10/10)
checklist: 1. I can explain what a class is in simple English (a blueprint/template).
2. I can explain what an object is (a real instance created from that blueprint).
3. I know the exact difference between a class and an object.
4. I can define what object state means (the data it currently knows).
5. I can define what object behavior means (the actions it can perform).
6. I know that one class can create an unlimited number of objects.
7. I understand that each object maintains its own independent state.
8. I can identify real-world entities (like User, Order, Product) from a requirement.
9. I can read a simple OOP program and accurately predict what it will print.
10. I can write a class and instantiate an object completely from scratch!

practiceProblems.title: Build the Student Profile System (Core)
practiceProblems.description:
Build the complete Student Profile program from scratch using classes and objects:

1. Define a `Student` class with fields: `name`, `age`, `course`, and `marks`.
2. Add a `displayProfile()` method that formats and prints the profile card.
3. In `Main`, instantiate Rahul (20, Java, 85.5) and Priya (21, Python, 91.0).
4. Call `displayProfile()` on both objects with a blank line between them.

practiceProblems.title: Add Pass/Fail Result Calculation
practiceProblems.description:
Add a business rule method to the `Student` class:

• Add a method `boolean isPassed()` which returns `true` if `marks >= 50.0`, otherwise `false`.
• In `Main`, test with a student who scored `45.0` (Failed) and another who scored `82.0` (Passed).
• Print: `Rahul passed: true | Karan passed: false`.
